analogy.p: Imagine the universe as a tall Jenga tower built to a plan: every block supports the ones above. Macbeth pulls the top block out (the king). A tower does not just lose one piece; the whole structure wobbles and eventually falls. That is why Shakespeare shows storms, strange animals and sleeplessness after Duncan dies. Where the analogy breaks down: a Jenga tower has no moral meaning, whereas the Jacobean universe was ordered by God’s will, so the collapse is also a judgement.
analogy.t: The Great Chain as a Jenga tower

bullets: Choose three or four contexts only: James I and divine right, the Great Chain of Being, the Gunpowder Plot and treason, witchcraft (covered in the next note). Depth beats breadth.
Always attach a context to a moment: Act and Scene, a quotation, an effect on the audience.
Use phrases such as “a Jacobean audience would have…”, “Shakespeare, writing for a king who…”, “this reflects the contemporary belief that…”.
Never claim a context as certain fact if historians dispute it (for example, exactly when and before whom Macbeth was first performed).
Remember the question may not mention context; you can still earn AO3 marks if the question asks about “ideas” or “the play as a whole”. Check the wording and mark scheme on your paper.

callouts.p: Quote, analyse the word, then add context as an explanation of effect: ‘…which a Jacobean audience, taught that the king was God’s deputy, would see as…’. This keeps AO2 and AO3 fused.
Weak: “James I was king and he believed in witches.” Strong: tie belief to a scene, a word and an audience reaction.

core.h: How to use context at grade 9 (AO3)
core.p: Context is not a list of historical facts placed in an introduction. AO3 rewards you when a fact explains why Shakespeare shapes a moment in a particular way or why a Jacobean audience would react differently from you. The test is simple: if you could delete the context sentence and the paragraph would still make sense, it is bolted on. A grade 9 answer uses context as part of the interpretation, typically in the middle of an analytical paragraph and tied to a specific word or moment.

Where it shows in the play
What to say

Witches as real threat to the state
Royal touch for the King’s evil
Act 4 Sc 3, English court
A true king heals, a tyrant harms

bullets: James was a published author: Daemonologie (1597) on witchcraft, and works on kingship including The True Law of Free Monarchies (1598) and Basilikon Doron (1599).
He believed he was descended from Banquo through the Stuart line; the play flatters this by showing Banquo as noble and promising him a line of kings.
He survived plots against his life in Scotland before 1603 and the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, so assassination was a real personal fear.
Shakespeare changes Banquo from the accomplice of Holinshed’s Chronicles into a loyal, suspicious friend; to make James’s supposed ancestor a murderer would have been dangerous.
The play is short and fast-moving, and spectacle such as the show of kings suits a royal audience, but be careful: it is often claimed Macbeth was staged at court, though this is not certain.

core.h: James I: the king in the audience
core.p: James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603 when Elizabeth I died childless, uniting the crowns in his person. Shakespeare’s acting company became the King’s Men, so James was effectively their patron. Writing a play set in Scotland, about a Scottish king, soon after a Scot took the English throne, was both topical and politically wise.

bullets: Duncan is “anointed” and sacred; Macbeth’s own conscience knows this in Act 1 Sc 7 (“his virtues will plead like angels”) and he fears for his soul.
Macbeth’s hesitation is partly fear of judgement “in this life”, but he still dismisses the afterlife for a moment (“We’d jump the life to come”).
Macduff’s language in Act 2 Sc 3 (“sacrilegious murder”) turns politics into religion.
Malcolm’s final words restore the crown “by the grace of Grace”, putting kingship back under God.
Macbeth becomes a “tyrant” and is called the “dead butcher”: a usurper without divine sanction, so the audience supports the rebels, not the king.

callouts.p: The belief that a monarch’s authority comes directly from God, so the king answers only to God and rebellion against him is a sin.
Shakespeare makes Duncan a good, gentle king so that the crime cannot be justified as tyrannicide.
callouts.t: Why the audience is on Duncan’s side

core.p: Divine right is the belief that a monarch is chosen by God and answers only to God. The coronation oil showed this: the king was “anointed”. Because the king was God’s representative, rebelling against him was not only treason but a sin that risked damnation. James argued this at length in his own writing, so a Jacobean audience would feel Macbeth’s crime as spiritual as well as political.

bullets: After the murder, nature behaves unnaturally: a dark day, horses eating each other (Act 2 Sc 4), an owl killing a falcon, a night of storms and strange cries (Act 2 Sc 3).
Inversion is the play’s signature idea: “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” (Act 1 Sc 1) sets up a world turned upside down.
Macbeth’s mind is also disordered: he cannot sleep (“Macbeth does murder sleep”), and sleep, a natural restorer, is denied him.
Lady Macbeth’s request to be “unsexed” (Act 1 Sc 5) also challenges the natural order of gender as Jacobeans understood it.
The chain is restored when Malcolm is crowned, a return to order that reassures the audience.

callouts.p: Disorder follows each key crime: Duncan’s murder (storm and darkness), Banquo’s murder (the ghost), Macduff’s family’s murder (England’s healing king in contrast). You can make a structural point that Shakespeare uses nature as a barometer.

core.p: The Great Chain of Being was the Elizabethan and Jacobean model of the universe: everything has a fixed place from God at the top, through angels, kings, nobles, commoners, animals, plants and minerals. Each link is connected, so tampering with one disturbs all. The idea gives Shakespeare a framework for showing the effects of Macbeth’s murder in nature, society and the mind.

bullets: The conspirators looked loyal until they were exposed; Duncan’s remark that you cannot read “the mind’s construction in the face” rings with this fear.

Macbeth says “False face must hide what the false heart doth know” at the end of Act 1 Sc 7 and his wife tells him to “look like th’ innocent flower, but be the serpent under’t”, which expresses exactly the kind of hypocrisy the authorities feared.
The Porter’s “equivocator” speech (Act 2 Sc 3) alludes to the doctrine of equivocation, linked to Catholic priests such as Henry Garnet, who was tried in 1606.
The Porter’s hell-gate scene turns Macbeth’s castle into hell, which supports the view that traitors serve the devil.
Macbeth is killed, and the traitor’s head is displayed by Macduff in the last scene, a reminder that Jacobean traitors were punished by public execution.

callouts.p: The play is usually dated to about 1606; say “around 1606” or “soon after the Gunpowder Plot”, not an exact day.

core.h: The Gunpowder Plot and fear of regicide
core.p: On 5 November 1605 a group of Catholic conspirators, led by Robert Catesby, planned to blow up the House of Lords at the State Opening of Parliament, killing King James. Guy Fawkes was caught guarding the gunpowder in the cellar. The plot caused national shock, and its discovery was celebrated with bonfires and sermons. When Macbeth was written soon afterwards, a play about regicide, treachery and hidden conspirators was extremely topical.

head: Plot feature
Echo in Macbeth
rows: Secret meetings and hidden plans
Lady Macbeth’s “look like th’ innocent flower”; the murder planned behind a welcoming face
Treason against a sacred king
Duncan’s murder as sacrilege
Fear of ambiguous speech
Equivocator; witches’ riddling prophecies; Macbeth’s misreading of “none of woman born”
Punishment of traitors
Cawdor executed at the start; Macbeth’s head displayed at the end

bullets: Flattery reading: Banquo’s line, the English king’s healing touch, Scotland restored under Malcolm.
Warning reading: Macbeth begins as a loyal hero, showing that the best subject can become the worst traitor if ambition goes unchecked.
Sympathy reading: audiences are drawn into Macbeth’s imagination (“Is this a dagger…”), so the play makes regicide frighteningly intelligible.
Shakespeare changes his source Holinshed: he makes Duncan more virtuous and Banquo loyal so that the Stuart king appears in a good light.
The “touch” scene in Act 4 Sc 3 describes the English king curing a disease called the King’s evil; James also touched for it, so this is an obvious compliment.

callouts.p: “A Jacobean audience may have seen… whereas a modern audience might see…” is a safe, accurate way to present alternative readings without overclaiming.

core.h: How Shakespeare engages the king: flattery and warning
core.p: Macbeth can be read as a play that reassures James: legitimate kings are God-given, usurpers fail, the descendants of Banquo survive and England has a healing king. But Shakespeare was also a sophisticated dramatist who gives the usurper the best soliloquies. This ambivalence is where grade 9 candidates earn the top marks by offering more than one reading.

bullets: ‘Shakespeare, writing for a king who believed in divine right, presents the murder as…’
‘The pathetic fallacy of the dark night would have confirmed the Jacobean belief that the natural world responds to royal disorder.’
‘Coming shortly after the Gunpowder Plot, the Porter’s equivocator would have unsettled an audience already alert to hidden treason.’
“By making Banquo noble, Shakespeare flatters James’s claimed ancestor while also…”
‘A modern audience may sympathise with Macbeth’s psychological torment, but a Jacobean one would see his damnation as just.’
Avoid: “In those days people were stupid and believed in witches.” Context is not condescension.
Avoid: attributing exact motives to Shakespeare as fact; use “perhaps”, “arguably”, “could suggest”.

callouts.p: On the extract question, check the mark scheme on your paper for how much weight AO3 has. Even if it is low, a single well-placed context point earns credit and deepens AO2.

core.h: Using context well: a checklist and a model sentence bank
core.p: Because context is easy to over-do, practise a small set of reliable sentence frames. Each links a historical fact to a specific effect on the audience, uses tentative verbs where appropriate, and returns to the writer’s methods.

plan: Duncan as ideal, sacred king (Act 1 Sc 4 and Act 1 Sc 7), divine right context
Regicide as cosmic crime (Act 2 Sc 3 and Sc 4), Great Chain of Being
Macbeth as tyrant and the corrupted crown (Act 3 and Act 4), contrast with Malcolm and Edward
Dynasty and flattery: Banquo’s line and the show of kings; alternative reading of ambiguity
Conclusion: Shakespeare’s purpose: reassurance and warning
essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents kingship in Macbeth. Refer to the context of the play in your answer.
essays.text:
Shakespeare presents kingship in Macbeth as a sacred trust, and Macbeth’s murder of Duncan as an offence not only against a man but against the whole order of creation. Writing for an audience ruled by James I, who argued in his own treatises that kings are God’s lieutenants on earth, Shakespeare makes divine right the moral backbone of the play.

Duncan is crafted as a virtuous king so that no audience can excuse the crime. Macbeth himself admits in his Act 1 Scene 7 soliloquy that Duncan “hath borne his faculties so meek”, a phrase whose Christian connotations of gentleness and sacrifice make the king a near-sacrificial victim. The very structure of that soliloquy, which moves from “If it were done” to a catalogue of reasons not to act, shows Macbeth knows he is about to commit what Jacobeans would see as the gravest sin. Shakespeare strengthens this by changing his source: in Holinshed, Duncan is a weak ruler, which makes the regicide more understandable; Shakespeare removes that excuse.

Once the murder is discovered, religious metaphor expresses the horror. Macduff calls the crime a breaking open of “the Lord’s anointed temple”, a metaphor that turns the king’s body into a consecrated building and reminds the audience of the anointing oil at a coronation. The disorder then spreads outwards. In Act 2 Scene 4 Ross describes the heavens as “troubled with man’s act”, and the Old Man reports an owl killing a falcon, a symbolic inversion of the hierarchy of the Great Chain of Being. Shakespeare therefore suggests that a disturbance at the top of the chain unsettles every level below it. A modern audience might read this as pathetic fallacy; a Jacobean audience, steeped in the idea that the king stands between God and his people, would take it as literal cosmic consequence.

Macbeth’s own reign becomes a counter-model of kingship. His “barren sceptre” and dread of Banquo’s line show a king who rules by fear rather than virtue, in contrast with Malcolm’s list of the “king-becoming graces” in Act 4 Scene 3. That scene is set in England, whose king can cure his subjects by touch, an echo of James’s own claim to the royal touch. Shakespeare thus allows divine right to be visibly validated in the play: a true king heals, a false king poisons.

Yet the play is more than royal flattery. The witches’ promise that Banquo will “get kings” and the apparition of a long line stretching “to the crack of doom” celebrate the Stuart descent from Banquo, but the same scene shows Macbeth’s horror at a future he cannot control. One could argue that Shakespeare is subtly reminding James that kingship can be corrupted by ambition, and that even a hero can become a tyrant. Written shortly after the Gunpowder Plot, when regicide was newly terrifying, the play lets the audience stare into the mind of the potential assassin and then watch him destroyed.

In conclusion, Shakespeare uses kingship to explore the fragile boundary between order and chaos. Macbeth is punished because he breaks a sacred chain, and Malcolm’s restoration reassures the audience that legitimate kingship will survive.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents kingship as a sacred trust that links human politics to cosmic order, so that Macbeth’s regicide is a violation of nature itself; but by making the usurper psychologically compelling he also lets the Jacobean audience look into the mind of the traitor that James most feared.
why: AO1: a conceptual thesis (kingship as sacred trust) sustained across the whole play rather than narrating events.
AO2: close zoom on single words (“anointed”, “meek”, “troubled”) with structural comment on the soliloquy and the shift to England in Act 4.
AO3: context is woven into the argument (divine right, Great Chain, royal touch, Stuart descent) and used to explain why the audience would respond as they do, not bolted on.
Alternative interpretation: the final paragraph weighs flattery against warning, which is the exploratory voice that earns the top band.
AO4: precise vocabulary (“connotations”, “inversion”, “counter-model”) and controlled sentence variety.

Macbeth as usurper whose reign brings disorder

exam.tip: Mark value is a best guess; check your paper. Hold a single conceptual thesis; do not tour the play act by act.

exam.tip: “How far” invites a judgement. Take a stance and qualify it.

Owl and falcon symbolism

mistakes.r: Select only the context that explains an effect in the extract or the play, and attach it to a moment and a quotation.
mistakes.w: Writing a history lesson: “James I was born in 1566…” with no link to the play.

mistakes.r: Use tentative language: “Shakespeare may have intended to flatter…”, “this would have appealed to…”.
mistakes.w: Saying “Shakespeare wanted to please James so he wrote…” as a certain fact.

mistakes.r: Say “written around 1606, soon after the Gunpowder Plot”. Dating and first performance are uncertain.
mistakes.w: Claiming the play was definitely written for the king’s court on a specific date.

mistakes.r: Show how it explains one moment, such as the owl killing the falcon, and what the audience would feel.
mistakes.w: Treating the Great Chain of Being as a list to name-drop.

mistakes.r: Weave context into the analysis paragraphs at the moment of the quotation.
Qualify: “many Jacobeans would have…”; mention that audiences vary.
mistakes.w: Assuming everyone in 1606 thought the same.

mistakes.r: Offer a second interpretation: flattery vs warning, villain vs victim.

quotes.a: Macduff turns Duncan’s body into a sacred building that has been broken into. The religious metaphor expresses divine right: the king is God’s chosen vessel, so murder is sacrilege, not merely treason. The word “anointed” recalls the oil used at a coronation. It could also show Macduff trying to find language big enough for a horror he cannot fully describe.
quotes.c: Divine right of kings: James I wrote that kings are God’s lieutenants on earth.
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 3, after the discovery of the body

quotes.a: The drunken Porter imagines a damned soul at hell-gate who lied with double meanings. “Equivocator” was a hot topic after the Gunpowder Plot because Catholic priests defended deliberately ambiguous answers under oath. The comic speech works as dramatic irony: the audience has just seen Macbeth and his wife lie in double meanings, and the witches’ prophecies are equivocations too.
quotes.c: Trial of Henry Garnet after the Gunpowder Plot (1606) and the debate about equivocation.
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 3, the Porter, early in the scene

quotes.a: The paradoxical prophecy gives Banquo what Macbeth most wants, a dynasty, which fuels Macbeth’s jealousy. The balanced antithesis (“kings” / “none”) is formal and riddling, typical of the witches. For a Jacobean audience it flatters James, who was traditionally said to descend from Banquo, so the line is both plot and politics.
quotes.c: James I’s claimed descent from Banquo through the Stuart line.
quotes.q: Thou shalt get kings, though thou be none
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 3, the witches to Banquo

quotes.a: Macbeth asks if Banquo’s line will stretch out “to the crack of doom”, meaning to the end of time. The apocalyptic image makes the royal succession look permanent, and the show of kings that follows ends with a figure holding mirrors, which many productions use to include the audience (and James) in the line. It is the play’s most direct nod to the royal house.
quotes.c: Stuart succession; James as the culmination of Banquo’s line.

quotes.a: Ross says the heavens themselves are disturbed by what humans have done. Personifying the sky as upset shows that regicide breaks the cosmic order, not just a political one. The pathetic fallacy is also structural: the unnatural darkness tells the audience that Macbeth’s crime is beyond human justice. One could argue it also shows that Scotland’s whole society is implicated.
quotes.c: Great Chain of Being: a disturbance at the top disturbs every level below.
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 4, Ross and the Old Man

quotes.a: The Old Man reports that a falcon, a noble hunting bird, was attacked and killed by an owl that normally only catches mice. The reversal of predator and prey mirrors Macbeth (a lower-status thane) killing Duncan. The omen reflects the Great Chain of Being: when the highest is struck down, nature inverts. “Mousing” also makes Macbeth sound small and base for all his greatness.
quotes.c: Hierarchy of nature mirrors hierarchy of society.
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 4, the Old Man’s report

quotes.a: Macbeth admits that Duncan has exercised his powers humbly, which makes the murder even more shameful. The line shows that Duncan is a legitimate and virtuous king, so Macbeth cannot excuse himself as a tyrant-slayer. “Meek” has Christian connotations, associating Duncan with sacrificial innocence. Shakespeare invented this characterisation; in the source Duncan is a weaker ruler.
quotes.c: Divine right: a good king is God’s agent, so killing him is damnable.

quotes.a: Malcolm lists virtues such as justice, truth and temperance that a good king should have. The compound adjective sets out a Jacobean checklist for ideal monarchy, against which Macbeth the tyrant is measured. The scene is set in England, whose pious king cures his subjects by touch, so Shakespeare may be complimenting James’s own claim to a healing touch.
quotes.c: Basilikon Doron (James’s advice on kingship) stresses virtue; the “King’s touch” for scrofula.
quotes.ref: Act 4 Sc 3, Malcolm testing Macduff in England

quotes.a: Duncan says there is no way to read a person’s character from their face, just before Macbeth arrives. The irony is bitter: Duncan trusted Cawdor and will trust Macbeth. It sets up the theme of appearance and reality, and the Jacobean fear that traitors hide behind loyal faces, a fear sharpened by the Gunpowder Plot, whose conspirators were gentlemen who looked like respectable subjects.
quotes.q: the mind’s construction in the face
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 4, Duncan on the traitor Cawdor

quotes.a: Ross says night is “strangling” the sun in daytime. The violent verb turns the sun into a victim, echoing Duncan’s murder, and the sun (a traditional symbol of kingship) is overpowered by darkness. The image extends the motif of darkness that began when Macbeth asked the stars to hide their fires. Ross’s line can also be read as the play’s moral verdict.
quotes.c: The king as sun of the nation, a Renaissance commonplace.
quotes.q: dark night strangles the travelling lamp
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 4, Ross, early in the scene
quotes.t: personification, metaphor, light and dark imagery

summary: Know who James I was, what divine right and the Great Chain of Being meant, how the Gunpowder Plot (1605) shaped fears about regicide and treason, and how to weave this context (AO3) into an argument about Macbeth rather than bolting it on.

terms.d: The belief that a monarch rules by God’s authority and is answerable only to God.
The hierarchical model of the universe from God down to minerals, in which each being has a fixed place.
Someone who takes a throne by force or without right.
Speaking in a way that is deliberately ambiguous or misleading, often to avoid telling a direct lie.
When nature reflects human emotion or events, such as storms after a murder.
Belonging to the reign of James I (1603 to 1625).
A drama in which a noble protagonist falls through a flaw or error, ending in suffering or death.
Blessed with holy oil at a coronation, marking a king as chosen by God.
